content:
MEETING INFO
Title: Arcadia Health x Redwood Inference — Security / Compliance Review (Private/VPC)
Date: May 13, 2025
Time: 3:02pm PT
Duration: 47 min
Recorded by: Fireflies.ai

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Avery Johnson (AE), Simran Kaur (Solutions Architect), Naomi Feldman (Security/Compliance)
Arcadia Health: Priya Desai (Security & Risk), Tom Nguyen (Platform Eng), Emily Hart (Compliance), Maya Rodriguez (Procurement Ops)

SUMMARY (auto-generated)
Arcadia reviewed Redwood’s security posture for a Private/VPC deployment, focusing on SOC 2 evidence, encryption/KMS key ownership, audit log requirements, and data retention. Redwood clarified expected boundaries between Redwood’s control plane and Arcadia’s VPC environment, and agreed to provide an evidence package under NDA. Arcadia asked that any public case study avoid sensitive architecture and region details and only use approved, generalized claims.

TOPICS
- SOC 2 Type II, security evidence and questionnaire workflow
- KMS / customer-managed keys, key ownership, envelope encryption
- Audit logs: fields, export, retention, and access controls
- Data retention / prompt logging policy in Private deployment
- Case study constraints (public marketing language, review + approval)

QUESTIONS (captured)
- Can Redwood support customer-managed KMS keys (CMK) in a VPC deployment, and who has access to decrypt?
- What audit log events are captured (auth, model invocation, config change), and can logs be exported to our SIEM?
- Are prompts/outputs retained by default in Private? If yes, for how long and where?
- Can Redwood provide SOC 2 report + bridge letter and a list of subprocessors used for the control plane?
- For a public case study, can we avoid naming cloud region, model names, or traffic volumes?

ACTION ITEMS (auto-generated)
- Redwood: send SOC 2 Type II report under NDA, plus subprocessor list and pen test summary.
- Redwood: share audit log schema + example export configuration.
- Arcadia: send security questionnaire + required evidence format.
- Both: align on case study redlines and approval workflow.

TRANSCRIPT

[00:00] Avery Johnson: Cool, I think folks are trickling in. Um, Priya, Tom, Emily, Maya — thanks for making the time. This is the security and compliance review for Redwood, specifically for the Private/VPC deployment option.

[00:14] Priya Desai: Yep. Thanks Avery. We have a bunch of standard questions. I also want to be explicit: anything we do publicly, like a case study, we need to be careful about details.

[00:25] Avery Johnson: Totally understood. I’ve got Simran here for architecture and Naomi from our security/compliance team for evidence and controls.

[00:34] Naomi Feldman: Hi everyone.

[00:35] Simran Kaur: Hey.

[00:38] Tom Nguyen: Hi.

[00:40] Emily Hart: Hello.

[00:41] Maya Rodriguez: Hey.

[00:45] Avery Johnson: Awesome. Quick agenda: we’ll do SOC 2 evidence requests, then encryption/KMS, audit logs, and then talk about what can and can’t go in a case study. Sound okay?

[00:56] Priya Desai: Works.

[01:00] Naomi Feldman: Great. Maybe I’ll start with SOC 2. We are SOC 2 Type II, latest report period ended Q1. We can share under NDA via our Trust portal. We also have a subprocessor list, and we can provide a control mapping for your questionnaire if you send it.

[01:19] Priya Desai: Okay. We’ll need the full report, not just an attestation letter. Also any bridge letter if the period doesn’t cover current.

[01:28] Naomi Feldman: Yep, we can provide the report and a bridge letter. We typically do that as a PDF with a signed statement.

[01:35] Emily Hart: And do you have ISO 27001?

[01:37] Naomi Feldman: We’re not ISO certified today. We map a lot of controls, but SOC 2 is the main one. We can share policies and evidence where needed.

[01:46] Priya Desai: Got it. We’ll send our questionnaire. It’s… it’s long. Sorry in advance.

[01:52] Naomi Feldman: (laughs) That’s normal.

[01:55] Tom Nguyen: I’m going to jump to deployment boundaries. For the Private/VPC, what runs in our VPC versus what’s in your control plane? I want to understand what data traverses.

[02:07] Simran Kaur: Yeah. So in our Private mode, the inference plane — GPUs, model runtime, request handling — runs inside your VPC. The control plane is optional: you can have a private control plane as well, but usually there is some Redwood-managed component for licensing, updates, and telemetry, depending on the configuration. We can do customer-managed networking and restrict egress.

[02:28] Tom Nguyen: When you say telemetry, is that prompts and responses?

[02:31] Simran Kaur: By default, no. We do not need prompt content to operate. Telemetry is like latency, error codes, token counts, model version, request IDs. Prompt/response logging is configurable and can be disabled.

[02:45] Priya Desai: I need that in writing. “Prompt content not required.”

[02:48] Simran Kaur: Yep, we’ll send a doc and we can put it in the SOW.

[02:55] Emily Hart: Also retention. If prompt logging is enabled, where is it stored and for how long?

[03:02] Simran Kaur: In Private, it would be stored in your environment — like your logging destination — because the inference plane is in your VPC. If you turn on body logging, you’d typically send it to your own S3 bucket or your SIEM. Redwood doesn’t persist it outside unless you explicitly configure an external sink.

[03:20] Priya Desai: Okay. Now KMS. We require customer-managed keys for encryption at rest. Can you support that?

[03:28] Simran Kaur: Generally yes. We support envelope encryption patterns. If you’re on AWS, you can use KMS CMKs. For the disks and object storage in your VPC, that’s your choice. For any Redwood-managed components, we can support customer-managed keys in some configurations, but we’ll need to confirm exact scope.

[03:46] Priya Desai: I don’t want “generally.” I want: who can decrypt, and who holds the keys.

[03:51] Naomi Feldman: For anything in your VPC, you own the KMS keys and policies. Redwood personnel do not have access to your CMK. Our access would be via IAM roles you grant, and we recommend least privilege. For Redwood-managed systems, encryption keys are managed by Redwood, unless a bring-your-own-key option is in the statement of work.

[04:13] Priya Desai: So today, BYOK is only for some parts.

[04:16] Naomi Feldman: Correct. We need to scope which components would remain Redwood-managed. If you require full BYOK end to end, we can push the architecture to fully customer-managed control plane. That tends to be heavier operationally.

[04:30] Tom Nguyen: For us, the inference plane is the sensitive part. The control plane can be okay, but it cannot see payload.

[04:37] Simran Kaur: That aligns with how we deploy it. Control plane doesn’t need payload. It’s more like config, model catalog metadata, rollout policies, and health.

[04:49] Priya Desai: Any chance you’re doing “support snapshots” that include memory dumps? I’ve seen vendors do that.

[04:55] Simran Kaur: Not by default. For deep debugging, if we need logs, we’d ask first. And we can redact. Also, in Private, you can restrict what we can access.

[05:05] Naomi Feldman: And we have an access policy: support access is time-bound, approved, and logged. We can provide that policy excerpt.

[05:14] Emily Hart: Speaking of logged. Audit logs. What do you provide for audit events? We need to track admin activity, config changes, and access.

[05:23] Simran Kaur: Yep. In Console, we have audit events like: user login, API key creation/rotation, RBAC changes, model deployment changes, routing policy changes, and also inference request metadata. For Private, we can export logs to your systems.

[05:41] Tom Nguyen: Is that like a JSON log stream? What fields?

[05:44] Simran Kaur: It’s JSON. Fields include timestamp, actor, action, resource, request_id, org_id, ip address, and sometimes diff payloads for config changes.

[05:57] Priya Desai: We require user identifiers. Like, if it’s SSO, we need the email or a stable subject.

[06:03] Simran Kaur: If SSO is enabled, we can include the SSO subject and email depending on your configuration. We also support SAML-based SSO with RBAC.

[06:14] Priya Desai: Is SSO required for Private?

[06:17] Naomi Feldman: Not required, but recommended. Some customers do local users with MFA, but enterprise standard is SSO.

[06:25] Maya Rodriguez: From procurement perspective, we also need a list of subprocessors. I know this is Private, but there’s still like support tools.

[06:33] Naomi Feldman: Right. We can provide the subprocessor list for our corporate systems and any managed control plane services. For your VPC components, that’s within your own AWS account.

[06:45] Priya Desai: Okay, evidence. SOC 2, pen test, vuln scanning. Can you share pen test results?

[06:52] Naomi Feldman: We can share an executive summary. Full report is usually restricted, but we can provide a letter attesting remediation status and the summary of findings.

[07:03] Priya Desai: That might be okay. We’ll see.

[07:06] Tom Nguyen: How do you handle patching? If you ship an appliance into our VPC, who patches it.

[07:12] Simran Kaur: It’s a mix. We can do managed updates where we push versioned releases, you approve a maintenance window, and we roll forward. Or you can do self-managed updates if you want full control. Most Private customers choose Redwood-managed updates but with approval gates.

[07:29] Emily Hart: And do you have an SLA for incident notification?

[07:33] Naomi Feldman: For enterprise contracts, yes: incident notification timelines and a named security contact. We can align to your requirements.

[07:42] Priya Desai: Alright. Now the tricky part: data. In Hosted systems we always ask: do you retain prompts, are they used for training? Here too.

[07:53] Naomi Feldman: We do not use customer data to train models. For Hosted, there are configurable retention options. For Private, since it’s in your environment, you control retention. We can operate without retaining payload.

[08:10] Priya Desai: Okay. But your team can access the box, potentially. What’s the access model.

[08:16] Simran Kaur: Access is via a bastion or VPN you provide, usually with session recording. We recommend that. We can also do “break glass” procedures with customer approval. Again: time-bound, audited.

[08:31] Tom Nguyen: Do you support customer-controlled audit of your access? Like we want CloudTrail events and we want to know when you run commands.

[08:38] Simran Kaur: If it’s in your AWS account, yes, you’d see CloudTrail. If we deploy via EKS, your cluster audit logs can capture kubectl actions. We can also provide a support role that’s read-only unless escalated.

[08:52] Priya Desai: Good.

[08:55] Avery Johnson: Quick check — Priya, does this match the review you need for your internal gate? Like, we’re trying to make sure we clear the security “go/no-go” for the design partner program.

[09:05] Priya Desai: Mostly. The key is: we need the SOC 2 report and we need clarity on KMS. Also audit logs schema. And we need assurance no payload leaves our VPC.

[09:18] Simran Kaur: We can provide a data flow diagram that shows payload stays in VPC. But for the public case study, we probably shouldn’t publish that full diagram.

[09:28] Priya Desai: Exactly.

[09:30] Emily Hart: Yeah, that’s where I wanted to go. Marketing keeps asking for “architecture diagrams.” We can do a generalized one, but it cannot show network topology, IP ranges, region, any vendor specifics beyond “VPC”.

[09:44] Avery Johnson: That’s aligned with our case study process. We can do a high-level box diagram: “Arcadia app” -> “Redwood Private inference in VPC” -> “logging to SIEM” etc.

[09:55] Priya Desai: And no mention of “we process PHI” or anything like that.

[09:58] Avery Johnson: Understood.

[10:01] Naomi Feldman: Also on public language: avoid stating exact control implementations like “customer uses KMS key ID X” obviously. But we can say “customer-managed keys” if approved.

[10:12] Tom Nguyen: And no exact metrics. Like p95 latency numbers could imply scale.

[10:18] Avery Johnson: We can phrase outcomes as ranges or relative improvements, subject to your approval.

[10:25] Priya Desai: If we do numbers, it’s only if we approve and it’s not tied to volume.

[10:29] Simran Kaur: Makes sense.

[10:32] Emily Hart: Back to audit logs. We need specific events: admin login, role changes, model deploy changes, key rotations, and config diff.

[10:41] Simran Kaur: We have most of that. Key rotations: for API keys and user tokens yes. For KMS keys, that’s in your KMS/CloudTrail. Config diff: we log the “before/after” for some settings; for others we log the action and the new value.

[10:58] Priya Desai: Can you export logs automatically? We use Splunk.

[11:02] Simran Kaur: Yes. Typical pattern is shipping JSON logs to an S3 bucket, and then Splunk pulls. We can also do syslog or HTTP sink, depending.

[11:15] Tom Nguyen: Any rate limit? If we do high throughput, audit logs could be heavy.

[11:20] Simran Kaur: We can tune. Also note: request-level logs can be sampled; admin audit logs are low volume.

[11:29] Priya Desai: Sampling is okay for request logs, not okay for admin.

[11:33] Simran Kaur: Yep, agreed.

[11:36] Naomi Feldman: And for access logs, we can provide a list of event types and fields. We’ll send an example schema.

[11:44] Maya Rodriguez: Can we also talk about where your employees are located? We have restrictions on support being US-only for some systems.

[11:52] Naomi Feldman: We can support US-only support staffing for certain tiers. It would be contractual and scheduling-based. For urgent incidents, we’d still try to honor it, but we need to define it in the support terms.

[12:08] Priya Desai: That’s important. At minimum, data access must be US-only.

[12:12] Simran Kaur: In Private, access is in your account. We can configure support role access and restrict who can assume it.

[12:22] Priya Desai: Okay.

[12:24] Tom Nguyen: Another question: encryption in transit. TLS termination — where does that happen.

[12:30] Simran Kaur: Usually at your load balancer inside VPC. We support TLS all the way to the gateway if required. Between services, we can do mTLS in-cluster depending on your service mesh.

[12:43] Tom Nguyen: Okay. And at rest: model weights, caches.

[12:47] Simran Kaur: Model weights are on encrypted volumes. KV cache is in GPU memory; it’s ephemeral. Any disk spill is optional and also encrypted.

[12:58] Priya Desai: You said “KV cash”?

[13:00] Simran Kaur: KV cache, sorry — key/value cache used by transformer inference.

[13:05] Priya Desai: Got it.

[13:08] Emily Hart: Do you log prompts by default anywhere? Like in error logs.

[13:12] Simran Kaur: We avoid logging prompt content. Sometimes stack traces can include snippets if upstream systems do it, but we strip request bodies at the gateway in Private. We can configure it to never log body.

[13:26] Priya Desai: Good.

[13:28] Naomi Feldman: We also have a secure SDLC policy, code review, dependency scanning, and incident response runbooks. Those are in our SOC 2.

[13:38] Priya Desai: Great.

[13:40] Avery Johnson: Could we talk briefly about your internal timeline? Like when do you need evidence to complete the security review?

[13:47] Maya Rodriguez: Procurement would like it this week to keep momentum.

[13:51] Priya Desai: Realistically, if we get the SOC 2 by end of week and the architecture doc, we can approve the POC start.

[14:01] Avery Johnson: Okay, that’s helpful.

[14:04] Tom Nguyen: I want to ask about “subprocessors” again. In Hosted we see vendors use OpenAI, etc. Here, what LLM models are used, and does anything call out.

[14:15] Simran Kaur: In Private, models run in your environment. No calls out to third-party model APIs. The only external dependency could be optional update checks or license validation, which can be pinned and routed privately.

[14:30] Tom Nguyen: So no AWS Bedrock involved.

[14:33] Simran Kaur: Not unless you choose to. Redwood is the inference runtime in your VPC.

[14:38] Priya Desai: That’s good. We’ve had bad experiences with vendors quietly calling external endpoints.

[14:45] Simran Kaur: Yep. We can provide an egress allowlist. And you can enforce no egress at the subnet level.

[14:55] Emily Hart: For case study language, can we say “no data leaves Arcadia’s VPC”?

[15:01] Priya Desai: Potentially, but we need to review exact wording. “No customer data” is broad.

[15:06] Naomi Feldman: We can phrase it as: “Inference requests are processed within Arcadia’s private cloud environment; payload is not transmitted to Redwood-hosted systems.” Something like that.

[15:18] Avery Johnson: We’ll propose and you can redline.

[15:21] Priya Desai: Perfect.

[15:24] Tom Nguyen: Another technical question: do you support dedicated tenant isolation in the control plane. Like, do we share a console with others.

[15:32] Simran Kaur: For Private, console can be single-tenant. For Dedicated hosted, we isolate compute but the console is multi-tenant logically with org separation. For Private, we can deploy the console in your VPC as well.

[15:47] Tom Nguyen: Okay.

[15:49] Priya Desai: Now, evidence requests: in addition to SOC 2, we need your data retention policy, IR policy, and subprocessor list. Also, any HIPAA alignment.

[16:01] Naomi Feldman: We don’t claim HIPAA compliance as a blanket statement. We can sign a BAA for certain deployments, and we can support the required safeguards. But we need to scope it.

[16:13] Priya Desai: Fine. We may not need a BAA for this phase, but don’t put HIPAA in marketing.

[16:18] Avery Johnson: Understood. We will not.

[16:21] Emily Hart: Thank you.

[16:23] Tom Nguyen: For audit logs, can we get “model version” and “policy version” attached to each request. Because we need traceability.

[16:31] Simran Kaur: Yes, we can attach model version IDs and route/policy IDs. We also have rollout IDs for canaries.

[16:41] Tom Nguyen: Great.

[16:43] Priya Desai: Are you doing any user content caching. Like prompt caching.

[16:48] Simran Kaur: We have prefix caching/KV caching. In Private, cache lives in memory in your environment. It’s not shared across tenants unless you configure it. We can set cache scopes per API key or per tenant header.

[17:03] Priya Desai: So potentially content sits in memory.

[17:06] Simran Kaur: Yes, ephemeral. If you consider that sensitive, we can scope cache TTL and disable cross-request caching.

[17:15] Priya Desai: Okay.

[17:17] Emily Hart: Can we include “audit logs” as a benefit in the case study? That’s not sensitive.

[17:22] Priya Desai: Benefits are fine. Implementation details not.

[17:26] Avery Johnson: Got it.

[17:28] Naomi Feldman: Also, for public case study, we recommend: no mention of exact cloud provider accounts, region, and no screenshots of dashboards unless scrubbed.

[17:39] Emily Hart: Yes please, no screenshots. Or if any, needs heavy redaction.

[17:44] Avery Johnson: Okay.

[17:46] Tom Nguyen: Quick compare: we’ve looked at Azure OpenAI and Bedrock. The issue was data boundary and retention. So if you can give us this VPC story, it helps.

[17:58] Simran Kaur: That’s exactly what Private is for.

[18:01] Priya Desai: Okay, I think we covered key areas. Naomi, can you confirm what you’ll send and how.

[18:08] Naomi Feldman: Yes. Assuming NDA, I’ll send: SOC 2 Type II report, bridge letter if needed, subprocessor list, and our security overview. Simran will send the Private deployment security architecture one-pager and audit log schema sample.

[18:27] Priya Desai: And please include: key ownership statement. Like who controls KMS keys.

[18:32] Simran Kaur: Yep.

[18:34] Maya Rodriguez: I’ll coordinate NDA if it’s not already in place. I think we have a mutual NDA but I’ll confirm.

[18:41] Avery Johnson: Thanks Maya. We have an NDA from the earlier discovery, but we’ll double-check scope.

[18:47] Emily Hart: One more: marketing approvals. For a case study, we need security review and then legal. It can take weeks.

[18:55] Avery Johnson: That’s okay. We’re planning a draft, then you review and we iterate.

[19:02] Priya Desai: Also, we may only approve anonymized case study. We’re not sure yet.

[19:08] Avery Johnson: Understood. We can do anonymized or named, your choice.

[19:13] Tom Nguyen: Okay.

[19:15] (crosstalk)

[19:16] Avery Johnson: Sorry, go ahead Priya.

[19:18] Priya Desai: Just to be clear: no mention of our internal systems, no mention of patient anything, no mention of specific compliance frameworks we use.

[19:29] Avery Johnson: Got it.

[19:31] Simran Kaur: And for our side, we need to avoid implying features that aren’t GA. So we’ll keep claims tight.

[19:38] Emily Hart: Good.

[19:40] Avery Johnson: Any other questions before we wrap?

[19:43] Priya Desai: Not now. Send the evidence and we’ll follow up.

[19:47] Tom Nguyen: Yeah, please send the audit log schema. That’s the biggest blocker for me.

[19:52] Simran Kaur: Will do.

[19:54] Avery Johnson: Great. I’ll send a recap email with the list of docs and owners. Thanks everyone.

[20:01] Priya Desai: Thanks.

[20:02] Emily Hart: Thank you.

[20:03] Tom Nguyen: Thanks.

[20:04] Naomi Feldman: Thanks.

[20:05] Simran Kaur: Bye.

NOTE: Fireflies transcript ended slightly early due to conferencing disconnect; remaining time in calendar slot was used for offline recap.
